yearsToFullBearing.note: Full production around years 12–13 in the general KZN guide. Cultivar, propagation, density and management affect actual output; mature ages do not automatically create an annual kg/tree curve.

source.quote: In pecans [Carya illinoinensis (Wangenh. K. Koch)], male (staminate) and female (pistillate) flowers occur on the same tree (monoecious) and exhibits heterodichogamy ... Therefore, trees were divided into two groups: “Protandrous” (Type I) which is when pollen from the male flowers is shed before the female flowers are receptive, and “Protogynous” (Type II), where female flowers are receptive to pollen before pollen is shed from the male flowers ... Compatible cultivars need to be in close proximity to each other for successful cross-pollination ... It is possible for fruit to set through self-pollination in the case of incomplete dichogamy, but this often results in smaller and lighter nuts ... Under self-pollination, pecan yield is 35 – 75% lower with nut quality severely reduced (Polles et al., 1980). Complete dichogamy will result in a self-sterile cultivar, as there is no overlap between pollen shed and pistil receptivity.
source.doc: Lötze, E., 'Literature Review: Factors influencing pollination of pecans for commercial production', published by SAPPA

pollination.note: Pecan is wind-pollinated and monoecious (male and female flowers on the same tree) but exhibits heterodichogamy — male and female flowers on a given tree mature at different times (Type I protandrous vs Type II protogynous) — so a single tree/cultivar alone generally cannot pollinate itself well or at all (many named cultivars are effectively self-sterile), and commercial orchards in South Africa are planted with complementary Type I x Type II cultivar combinations. Self-pollination is possible in some cultivars with incomplete dichogamy but yields 35-75% less with poorer nut quality — hence 'needs-cross-pollinator' rather than 'partly-self-fertile' or 'self-fertile'.

source.quote: Cross-pollination increases yields by 52% when compared with open pollination. ... Cross-pollination increases yields by 48.5% and improves nut quality (size and kernel weight). ... Genotyping of macadamia kernel to determine pollen parents: A4 was highly outcrossing (97%), 695 was 64% outcrossed, 816 41% outcrossed and 814 showed 10% outcrossing. ... Results demonstrated the critical role of honeybee colonies in macadamia orchards, with the absence of bees resulting in only 30% production in both cultivars.
source.doc: SAMAC (South African Macadamia Growers' Association), 'What have we learned 2024' research summary newsletter

pollination.note: Changed from needs-cross-pollinator to partly-self-fertile in editor review: the same SAMAC summary measures 10-97% outcrossing by kernel genotyping (so some nuts are selfed) and says cross-pollination RAISES yield by about half, which is a partly self-fertile tree, not one that needs a pollinator to bear. SAMAC's own research summaries show macadamia is capable of self/open pollination (a cultivar-dependent 10-97% outcrossing rate was measured by kernel genotyping, and orchards without managed bee colonies still achieved 30% of full production) but that yield is substantially higher (48.5-52% more) with cross-pollination (interplanted cultivars) and managed honeybee colonies (industry recommends at least two hives/ha). This mixed picture — fruit set possible alone, but commercially reliant on cross-pollination/bee activity — is why 'needs-cross-pollinator' (the industry-recommended practice) rather than 'self-fertile' was chosen, though 'partly-self-fertile' is also defensible given the cultivar-dependent self/open-pollination yield floor; see this nuance rather than treating the choice as clear-cut.

yieldKgPerTree.note: Same-trial arithmetic at the initial 200 trees/ha: 20,000 kg/ha / 200 = 100 kg/tree at age 6; sustainable average 22,500 kg/ha / 200 = 112.5 kg/tree. At age 3, 10,000 kg/ha / 200 = 50 kg/tree equivalent. These are average-equivalent reference values for the named Hass/Duke 7 orchard conditions, not measured individual-tree yields or default production for a different density, cultivar, climate or management. Intermediate ages are not inferred.

windows.region: South Africa (overall, all regions combined)

source.quote: South Africa boasts five major growing regions...enable growers to supply the markets with the latest varieties from November to May.
source.doc: South African Table Grape Industry (SATI) — 'About' page

source.quote: Hermaphroditic (perfect) flowers were a key trait in grapevine domestication, enabling a drastic increase in yields due to the efficiency of self-pollination in the domesticated grapevine (Vitis vinifera L. ssp. vinifera).
source.doc: Zou, Massonnet, Minio et al., 'Multiple independent recombinations led to hermaphroditism in grapevine', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Vol. 118, No. 15, e2023548118 (2021)

pollination.note: This is a general (not South Africa-specific) peer-reviewed genetics/domestication paper, used because it directly and explicitly states that cultivated Vitis vinifera (the domesticated subspecies grown as table grapes, as opposed to wild dioecious V. vinifera ssp. sylvestris) bears hermaphroditic, self-pollinating flowers — i.e. does not require a separate pollinator vine. No SA-specific source contradicting or refining this general botanical fact was found; SA table-grape cultivar sheets/enterprise budgets checked in this session (e.g. the Elsenburg Flame Seedless budget) did not mention any cross-pollination requirement, consistent with self-fertility.

supplementaryReferences.note: Year 4 commercial budget: 4,400 cartons/ha at 4.5 kg/carton = 19,800 kg/ha. The source does not provide matched vines/ha or row/vine spacing, so no kg/vine is derived. supplementaryReferences.title: South African trial harvest duration and native yields

source.quote: seven to eight months after planting
source.doc: Gatabazi et al. (2022), Scientia Horticulturae 304:111353

supplementaryReferences.note: Pretoria Hillcrest rain-shelter trial, 2015/16 and 2016/17, drip irrigation on sandy clay loam. Commercial ginger Z. officinale at eight months: 38.3 t/ha fresh and 8.8 t/ha dry rhizomes in the well-watered treatment; African ginger was a different species with different values. No matched plant density is supplied, so no kg/plant or household drying conversion is derived. The abstract says open field, while Methods specifies rain shelter; conditions are retained.

supplementaryReferences.title: Cultivar-dependent pollen compatibility

source.quote: 458 self-compatible and 101 self- incompatible
source.doc: dos Santos et al. (2007), Evidence of late-acting self-incompatibility in Acca sellowiana, Revista Brasileira de Fruticultura 29(1)

supplementaryReferences.note: Primary Brazilian germplasm experiment found both compatibility classes. Biological evidence supports checking the actual cultivar and compatible pollen, not assigning one universal species category or copying its calendar to South Africa.

supplementaryReferences.title: South African research context

source.quote: Lesser-known exotic crops being evaluated are pitanga, feijoa
source.doc: South African Yearbook 2003/04, ARC tropical/subtropical crop research

supplementaryReferences.note: Government confirms ARC evaluated feijoa; no trial result, cultivar, harvest month or yield follows from this mention.

care: Check the actual cultivar's pollen needs. A primary trial includes self-compatible and self-incompatible plants.
Record local ripe picking dates and output. Foreign cultivar seasons do not establish a South African season.
purchase: Ask the nursery to name the cultivar or identify a seedling and provide local fruiting and compatible-pollen evidence. 'Fruit Salad Tree' is a common sales label and does not identify a tested cultivar.

supplementaryReferences.title: Young flower-bud food use

source.quote: The young flower buds can be eaten
source.doc: SANBI PlantZAfrica: Aloidendron dichotomum

supplementaryReferences.note: The edible product is the young flower bud. June–July flowering does not establish the exact pre-opening picking dates, first bud-bearing age or edible kg/plant.

care: Match cultivation to this arid-land tree and well-drained conditions.
Record young-bud picking separately from flowering or ornamental growth.
purchase: Obtain correctly identified legal nursery stock and local growing advice. No food-yield cultivar or maturity curve is verified.

harvest.name: Pineapple
harvest.product: fruit; keep whole fruit and processed portions separate

source.quote: Can vary tremendously, but a cycle time of 18 months is normal at Hluhluwe.
source.doc: KZN DARD, Fruit and Nut Production in KZN (2006), Pineapple: Bearing Age

yearsToFirstCrop.note: Hluhluwe production-cycle reference: 18 months / 12 = 1.5 years. The source explicitly says cycle length varies greatly. Starting material, cultivar, weather and flower initiation matter; this is neither a universal first-harvest date nor a 12-month annual yield.

supplementaryReferences.title: Hluhluwe crop-cycle output

source.quote: Yields (t/ha) Conservative: 50 Average: 60 to 75 Good: 80
source.doc: KZN DARD, Fruit and Nut Production in KZN (2006), Pineapple

supplementaryReferences.note: Regional hectare reference: conservative 50 t/ha, average 60–75 t/ha, good 80 t/ha per production crop. The same page describes a normal 18-month Hluhluwe cycle. These are not kg/plant/year or a forecast for a household planting.

supplementaryReferences.title: Cultivar and renewal choice

source.quote: Queen – Suckers planted at 120 000 to 150 000 plants per hectare tend to give optimum yields, but need to be re-established after the plant crop. ... Smooth Cayenne - mainly processing, weight 2kg ... Queen - mainly fresh market, weight 0.75kg
source.doc: KZN DARD, Fruit and Nut Production in KZN (2006), Pineapple: Spacing and Cultivars

supplementaryReferences.note: Queen and Smooth Cayenne serve different uses. The guide's example fruit weights (Queen 0.75 kg; Smooth Cayenne 2 kg) are cultivar descriptions, not annual yields per plant. Queen is re-established after the plant crop in this system.

supplementaryReferences.title: Climate and calendar conditions

source.quote: Plants are frost sensitive. ... Good drainage is essential ... In the warmer production area of Hluhluwe there is year-round planting. In cooler areas planting is restricted to the warmer months
source.doc: KZN DARD, Fruit and Nut Production in KZN (2006), Pineapple: Climate and Planting Times

supplementaryReferences.note: Frost sensitivity and drainage constrain the site. Year-round planting at Hluhluwe is a planting reference, not an all-year household picking window; cooler sites use warmer planting months.

productionGuidance.products: Pineapple fruit; whole fruit and processed portions have different weights.
care: Use a warm, frost-free, well-drained site. The KZN production reference is Hluhluwe; it does not establish suitability throughout South Africa.
Record planting and actual picking dates. Year-round commercial planting or marketing does not mean every planted pineapple gives fruit in every month.
purchase: KZN guide: Queen is a fresh-fruit candidate; Smooth Cayenne is mainly a processing candidate. Confirm clean crowns/suckers, local suitability and crop-cycle advice with a nursery. Queen re-establishment after the plant crop belongs in the future plan.

supplementaryReferences.title: Waterblommetjie food product and establishment

source.quote: Only the flowers and buds are used.
source.doc: SANBI PlantZAfrica: Aponogeton distachyos

supplementaryReferences.note: Western Cape pond food; vigorous winter/spring flowering and winter shop availability are qualitative seasonal evidence, not a numeric picking calendar. Seedlings reach flowering size in one season under ideal conditions, not a universal age-in-years guarantee.

supplementaryReferences.title: Ideal seedling establishment

source.quote: flowering size in one season
source.doc: SANBI PlantZAfrica: Aponogeton distachyos

supplementaryReferences.note: Qualitative ideal-condition establishment duration; it is not inserted into a generic tree-age curve.

care: Start tubers in loam in shallow pond water; move deeper into sun after strong growth.
Record edible flowers/buds and pond area. Dormant tubers resume growth as autumn water returns in the winter-rainfall cycle.
purchase: Obtain correctly identified pond plants. Confirm local pond conditions and actual picking dates; no pond-area yield or planting density is sourced.

harvest.name: Rooibos
harvest.product: young shoots for dried rooibos tea

windows.region: Cederberg / Western Cape winter-rainfall commercial rooibos

source.quote: from December through April
source.doc: SANBI PlantZAfrica: Aspalathus linearis

source.quote: 12- 18 months
source.doc: SANBI PlantZAfrica: Aspalathus linearis

yearsToFirstCrop.note: First commercial cutting readiness at 12–18 months in the described Cape production system. The account discusses sowing and transfer to plantations but does not explicitly define whether the clock starts at sowing or planting out. Confirm starting stock and timing locally. This is tea-shoot establishment, not fruit-tree bearing.

supplementaryReferences.title: Commercial tea cutting cycle and product

source.quote: young branches
source.doc: SANBI PlantZAfrica: Aspalathus linearis

supplementaryReferences.note: Selected commercial rooibos forms in the Cederberg winter-rainfall region are cut annually December–April, retaining older branches. Cut shoots are chopped, bruised, oxidised and dried. Fresh shoot kg and dried tea kg are separate products. The account describes replacement after up to five harvest years, not a mature kg/plant curve.

productionGuidance.products: young shoots for dried rooibos tea
care: Match planting to acidic, sandy winter-rainfall soils and locally suitable rooibos forms.
Keep fresh-cut shoot weights separate from processed dried tea; record the actual processing output.
purchase: Ask a local rooibos nursery or adviser for correctly identified, locally proven planting material. The Cape cycle is not a nationwide tea forecast.

supplementaryReferences.title: Documented leaf food use

source.quote: Leaves have been eaten as spinach by the local people.
source.doc: SANBI PlantZAfrica: Asystasia gangetica subsp. micrantha

supplementaryReferences.note: The article explicitly identifies the catalogue subspecies and edible leaves. Spring/summer flowering is not a leaf-picking calendar.

care: Use a moist growing position, with semi-shade or sun where water is adequate.
Control rooted runners so this fast groundcover does not smother neighbouring plants.
purchase: Buy correctly identified subspecies material. Record actual leaf-cutting dates and weights; no local yield variety or first-cutting duration is verified.

harvest.name: Powder-puff tree
harvest.product: young leaves reported edible — specialist review needed

supplementaryReferences.title: Edible-part and safety review

source.quote: The young leaves are edible
source.doc: SANBI PlantZAfrica, barringtonia-racemosa

supplementaryReferences.note: The same source reports poison in seeds, bark, wood and roots. Guava-like fruit appearance is not evidence of edible fruit.

supplementaryReferences.title: Poisonous parts must remain visible

source.quote: The seeds, bark, wood and roots contain the poison saponin
source.doc: SANBI PlantZAfrica, barringtonia-racemosa

supplementaryReferences.note: The account records fish-stunning use. No such use is recommended, and no household fruit food claim is made.

productionGuidance.products: young leaves reported edible — specialist review needed
care: Keep this tree in mapped inventory and do not count it as household food until identity and a safe edible-leaf preparation are reviewed.
SANBI describes humid coastal/estuarine conditions and no tolerance of even mild frost.
purchase: Ask a specialist nursery about lawful provenance and local site fit. Resolve the food-use question before purchasing it as a household crop.

supplementaryReferences.title: Leaf vegetable identity and warm-climate culture

source.quote: edible leaves
source.doc: UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions: Tropical Spinaches

supplementaryReferences.note: Florida extension confirms Malabar spinach as a warm-climate leaf vegetable. Its Florida planting and harvest calendar is not a South African calendar.

supplementaryReferences.title: Cultivation context

source.quote: trellis or fence
source.doc: UF/IFAS: Cultivation of Malabar Spinach in Florida

supplementaryReferences.note: Foreign extension reference for support, seed/cutting propagation and warm, moist conditions; no Florida months are imported into the South African plan.

supplementaryReferences.title: Optimal from-seed cutting-cycle reference — Florida extension

source.quote: around 70 days from seed in optimal conditions
source.doc: UF/IFAS: Florida Cultivation Guide for Malabar Spinach, Harvest and Storage

supplementaryReferences.note: The extension guide reports maturity around 70 days from seed under optimal conditions, followed by hand trimming leaves and young stems. This foreign optimal-condition duration is supplementary; no South African planting date, exact month window or generic tree-age value is inferred.

care: Provide climbing support and adequate moisture in a warm growing position.
Record successive leaf harvests by planting batch rather than using tree-age production.
purchase: Obtain labelled Basella alba material. A South African regional cultivar, kg/plant benchmark and dated picking window remain unverified.

supplementaryReferences.title: Edible part and local use

source.quote: The fruit is edible, very sweet in taste
source.doc: SANBI PlantZAfrica, berchemia-discolor

supplementaryReferences.note: January–July is fruit appearance in SANBI's account, not an explicit ripe-picking interval.

supplementaryReferences.title: Fruit-development duration has context

source.quote: 4-5 months from flower fertilization to fruit ripening
source.doc: World Agroforestry, Agroforestree Database, Berchemia discolor

supplementaryReferences.note: This is flower-to-fruit development, not years from planting. Its South African January–July fruiting statement is not an observed household picking window.

care: Use frost-free conditions: SANBI describes frost sensitivity despite drought resistance, with natural low-altitude riverbank bushveld in northern KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga and Limpopo.
purchase: Ask for Berchemia discolor, not red ivory (B. zeyheri). Record actual local ripe-picking months.

supplementaryReferences.title: Edible part and local use

source.quote: The fruits are used in traditional dishes
source.doc: SANBI PlantZAfrica, boscia-albitrunca

supplementaryReferences.note: SANBI also records flower-bud pickle use. Root porridge/coffee references are not instructions to harvest roots or a complete preparation guide.

care: This hardy, drought-resistant tree occurs in drier southern African regions.
SANBI reports that leaf browsing can taint cattle milk. No feed ration is recommended.
purchase: Ask for correctly identified, lawfully sourced stock and check current protected-tree collection requirements before harvesting existing wild trees.

harvest.name: Pigeon pea
harvest.product: dry grain or green immature seed; fodder is a separate product

supplementaryReferences.title: SA cultivar maturity and grain trial

source.quote: Days to maturity
source.doc: Mathews, Silim and Saxena: ICPN 8 (2001), Tables 1–2, printed pp37–38

supplementaryReferences.note: Malekutu, Mpumalanga, 1998/99; rainfed mid-December sowing, sandy loam, no fertiliser. Paired days after planting / grain kg/ha: ICPL 88039 127 / 1823; ICPL 85010 129 / 1525; ICPL 87091 140 / 1299; ICPL 87051 193 / 978; ICEAP 00053 231 / 918. Grain differences within each trial were not significant. Visually checked Tables 1–2 (PDF pp43–44). These are dry-grain observations, not green-seed picking dates or nationwide yield defaults.

supplementaryReferences.title: Tentative newer ARC planting comparison

source.quote: Tentatively, Variety 2 (ICEAP01284) can be recommended
source.doc: Bello, Mofokeng and du Toit: SA Graan/Grain, October 2021, pp56–57

supplementaryReferences.note: Potchefstroom 2020/21, good rainfall season: ICEAP01258 versus ICEAP01284 and 22 October versus 25 November sowing. ARC tentatively favours ICEAP01284 in late October and calls for further agro-ecological trials. Exact yield values were not taken from graph bars. Confirm current seed availability; this is not a national cultivar recommendation.

supplementaryReferences.title: Green seed is timed from flowering

source.quote: Green pods: Harvest 30-35 days after flowering
source.doc: DAFF: Legume poster, pigeon-pea column, Harvesting row

supplementaryReferences.note: The interval starts at flowering, not sowing. Dry-grain harvest is a separate pod-maturity stage. The broad marketing period does not mean that one planting supplies food continuously.

productionGuidance.products: dry grain or green immature seed; fodder is a separate product
care: Record green immature seed and dry grain separately; fodder biomass cannot be counted as household food kg.
Match the selected duration type and sowing date to local frost, rainfall and water availability; the trials retain their own conditions.
purchase: Discuss the named SA trial cultivars with a local seed supplier or extension adviser. Current purchase availability and suitability for this site are unverified; do not substitute a cultivar silently.

windows.region: KwaZulu-Natal

source.quote: The cropping season usually extends from about April to January, with a peak from September to November.
source.doc: KwaZulu-Natal Department of Agriculture and Rural Development, 'Fruit and Nut Production in KZN' (Horticultural Advisory Notes), section 1.6 Papaya, 'Bearing age'

source.quote: first crop is generally produced about 18 months later
source.doc: KZN DARD, Fruit and Nut Production in KZN, Bearing age

yearsToFirstCrop.note: KZN typical first crop after planting, about 18 months. The same paragraph reports 9–11 months under favourable Makhathini Flats conditions. This is a typical regional reference, not a minimum or guarantee.

supplementaryReferences.title: Plantation renewal

source.quote: The economic life of a plantation is only about 4-5 years.
source.doc: KZN DARD, Fruit and Nut Production in KZN (2006), Papaya: Bearing age

supplementaryReferences.note: The KZN guide gives about 4–5 years as the economic life of a plantation. Review replanting in the future plan; this commercial renewal reference does not mean every household plant dies at five or starts full production then.

supplementaryReferences.title: Regional hectare output

source.quote: Yields (t/ha) Conservative: 10 to 15 Average: 20 to 25 Good: 30
source.doc: KZN DARD, Fruit and Nut Production in KZN (2006), Papaya: Yields

source.quote: In pecans [Carya illinoinensis (Wangenh. K. Koch)], male (staminate) and female (pistillate) flowers occur on the same tree (monoecious) and exhibits heterodichogamy ... Therefore, trees were divided into two groups: “Protandrous” (Type I) which is when pollen from the male flowers is shed before the female flowers are receptive, and “Protogynous” (Type II), where female flowers are receptive to pollen before pollen is shed from the male flowers ... Compatible cultivars need to be in close proximity to each other for successful cross-pollination ... It is possible for fruit to set through self-pollination in the case of incomplete dichogamy, but this often results in smaller and lighter nuts ... Under self-pollination, pecan yield is 35 – 75% lower with nut quality severely reduced (Polles et al., 1980). Complete dichogamy will result in a self-sterile cultivar, as there is no overlap between pollen shed and pistil receptivity.
source.doc: Lötze, E., 'Literature Review: Factors influencing pollination of pecans for commercial production', published by SAPPA

pollination.note: Pecan is wind-pollinated and monoecious (male and female flowers on the same tree) but exhibits heterodichogamy — male and female flowers on a given tree mature at different times (Type I protandrous vs Type II protogynous) — so a single tree/cultivar alone generally cannot pollinate itself well or at all (many named cultivars are effectively self-sterile), and commercial orchards in South Africa are planted with complementary Type I x Type II cultivar combinations. Self-pollination is possible in some cultivars with incomplete dichogamy but yields 35-75% less with poorer nut quality — hence 'needs-cross-pollinator' rather than 'partly-self-fertile' or 'self-fertile'.

source.quote: Cross-pollination increases yields by 52% when compared with open pollination. ... Cross-pollination increases yields by 48.5% and improves nut quality (size and kernel weight). ... Genotyping of macadamia kernel to determine pollen parents: A4 was highly outcrossing (97%), 695 was 64% outcrossed, 816 41% outcrossed and 814 showed 10% outcrossing. ... Results demonstrated the critical role of honeybee colonies in macadamia orchards, with the absence of bees resulting in only 30% production in both cultivars.
source.doc: SAMAC (South African Macadamia Growers' Association), 'What have we learned 2024' research summary newsletter

pollination.note: Changed from needs-cross-pollinator to partly-self-fertile in editor review: the same SAMAC summary measures 10-97% outcrossing by kernel genotyping (so some nuts are selfed) and says cross-pollination RAISES yield by about half, which is a partly self-fertile tree, not one that needs a pollinator to bear. SAMAC's own research summaries show macadamia is capable of self/open pollination (a cultivar-dependent 10-97% outcrossing rate was measured by kernel genotyping, and orchards without managed bee colonies still achieved 30% of full production) but that yield is substantially higher (48.5-52% more) with cross-pollination (interplanted cultivars) and managed honeybee colonies (industry recommends at least two hives/ha). This mixed picture — fruit set possible alone, but commercially reliant on cross-pollination/bee activity — is why 'needs-cross-pollinator' (the industry-recommended practice) rather than 'self-fertile' was chosen, though 'partly-self-fertile' is also defensible given the cultivar-dependent self/open-pollination yield floor; see this nuance rather than treating the choice as clear-cut.

assumptions: Projection, not a harvest promise. Vegetables and staples repeat only saved recurring sowings; dated and existing crops happen once.
Vegetable and staple crop-cycle kilograms are counted in the year of first picking, not divided into monthly quantities. Carry-in harvests need actual records.
Vegetable and staple estimates hold bed area, sowings and crop benchmarks constant. Revise the plan if growing trees change shade, water or available bed space.
Tree ages run from planting on this site. Separate older and younger plants into age groups. Research first-crop ages are references, not guaranteed dates.

Tree kg are your farm or nursery assumptions per plant per year. Values hold until the next age you enter; no growth multiplier is invented. A range covers changes within the year. Review the schedule as plants age.
Check that the variety, local climate, pollination, water and care match your yield assumptions. Ages alone do not establish site suitability or survival.
Known subtotals leave out missing yields. Eggs, meat, milk, fish and honey are not included in these crop kg totals. Picking months and food-gap checks still need local confirmation.
